utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, before turning to the documents themselves, or some of the documents, two -- or one or two questions for you. I'm not suggesting that the phrases I'm about to use are academic or terms of science, if you will, but as part of your work with not only these documents but documents in general, do you consider what might be called the internal consistency of the documents and the external consistency of the documents, and if so, can you explain that a bit?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me begin, if you don't mind, with the -- what you might call the external consistency. This is what I think I was getting at yesterday in one of the later answers. Basically, making an inquiry into the external consistency of a document involves comparing it to other available documentary evidence and trying to establish whether there are any sorts of contradictions or, this probably isn't the right word but corroborations, consistencies, between them, of format, registration, style, more broadly content. So one often has, in an archive of this scale and degree of detail, numerous documents that bear on the same or related events. And one can see, you know, especially as the quantity of material you look at becomes quite large, whether or not they hang together, again to use a non-technical term. The internal consistency is a little more elusive, but you basically look at the document and see if there is -- again, to use a non-technical term, anything fishy about it. There were a very, very small number of documents that I saw that indicated that they had been altered in one fashion or another, and really the only one that I can recall was the subject of fairly extensive testimony in my earlier appearance, which I understand has been circulated. It was a document where the date had been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, just so the record is clear and so there is no confusion about this, this was testimony that you gave in the Kordic case, and one particular document came up about whether some information or a date had been altered, but it's not one of the documents included in the Tuta-Stela case, as far as you know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. If there's anything more you want to add to that part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's actually I think a good example in the initial version of the document in question. Two things caught one's attention. That was the absence of an order number in other documents which ordinarily had an order number. I had seen dozens, if not more, documents from the same author, all of which bore regular order numbers. And the second thing was the document in question had what was typed or computer printed, and yet the date was written in by hand. I later found different versions from different sources, those sources being from the archive itself. The original had been exhibited from an unknown source in yet a third case. And those bore an order number which did not match the date in question. And I was eventually able to establish by consulting a log book what the correct date was. And that was also borne out by the content and some other corroborating documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. All right. I think with that, let's turn to some of the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could assist me with having the binder marked "Selected Zagreb Archive Documents" placed before the witness, please. Mr. President, as I forecast yesterday afternoon, what I propose to do now is to go through a sampling of these documents so the Chamber can have an idea of what these documents look like, certainly not all of them by any means. But to take you through a few of them so you can see what type of documents are included in this collection. In looking at the documents, the Chamber might also have questions for Mr. Prelec that he can, perhaps, assist the Chamber on if that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, if you could turn in your binder and I could direct the courtroom's attention first to Exhibit 249, which, again, I'm unfortunately not able to tab this many sets of documents. If you leaf down until the lower right corner, most of the exhibit numbers will appear. And if you find 249. Again, just to keep -- to remind us of some of the things you said yesterday, if you look at the original of that document, that is the B/C/S version, do you see an archive stamp on that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's up in the upper right corner of the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this is a report or an order from the HVO Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic. And I would like to just briefly direct your attention to paragraphs numbered 1, 2, and 3. Could you just read those, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you prefer I read them in the original or in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For these purposes, Mr. Prelec, I think you can just read it in the English language. This is primary just to highlight and assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I order, one, create a company as per establishment enclosed from the members of Juka Prazina's units who have come back from Mount Igman. Two, appoint Mr. Juka Prazina as the commander of the unit. Three, issue HVO ID cards to all unit members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And this is, again, dated the 16th of February, 1993. And on the original version, you see such things as various stamps and markings as having been apparently received or logged or that sort of thing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you please turn next to Exhibit 301.1, which we used as an example of the stamp yesterday. I'll just direct your attention to a couple of things. Do you see that this is a report from Zeljko Siljeg dated the 16th of April, 1993. And if I direct your attention to the paragraph numbered 2, read just that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Establish a wire connection with facilities in Boksevica, Pisvir, Sovicka Vrata and the command of the Mijat Tomic Battalion in the village of Doljani."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you please then turn to paragraph number 7 on the following page and read that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Coordinating with Tuta is being done through the Posusje unit on Sovicka Vrata."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I ask you to turn to Exhibit 314, this is a -- appears to be a report from a battalion commander Stipe Pole, dated in Doljani on the 19th of April, 1993, and could you just read the first paragraph, first two paragraphs, please?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The mopping-up operation in the village of Sovici is nearing its end. Another three members of the BH army surrendered this morning and in the evening we captured one other man above Doljani. Consequently the number of prisoners" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please hold on. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe these documents will eventually speak for themselves, so I object to the witness just reading the paragraphs. They speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, unless there is very important matters, we could hear it, so you just may direct to the documents and the pages, and we could read it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, we can do that either way. There is -- I can jump to another couple specific items where maybe the witness could explain something specific. Again, I know there is a large volume of documents and I just simply was trying to assist the Chamber, give you a feel, kind of an introductory, if I can use that term, feel for what the documents look like. But I understand -- counsel is, of course, right: You can read the documents yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With that in mind, Mr. Prelec, why don't we turn to a particular item, 333.1, which is, I think, just the next document. And first off, again, specifically, if you look at that document, can you tell us whether that has an archive stamp?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to ask, I think on this one, if the usher could provide -- I don't know if it's possible to get an extra copy -- well, we can use the witness's copy. If the witness could also be provided Exhibit 56 at this time. Exhibit 56 could be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, would you look at Exhibit 333.1 and compare it to what you see on the overhead as 56, at least the translation of Exhibit 56? Looking at those two documents, can you tell us whether the text of those two documents are either identical or virtually identical?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They appear to be very similar. There are what I assume to be changes of phrasing that originate from translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Would you look at the B/C/S version of Exhibit 333.1? And perhaps that could be placed -- maybe probably the easiest thing to do if I could suggest is to remove that from your notebook for a moment and put that on the ELMO. Now, if everyone -- if I can just ask the courtroom to focus its attention on that for a moment, and there again, we have the archive stamp up in the right -- upper, right corner?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you also --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the usher please keep that document at hand but also put on, please, B/C/S version of Exhibit 56?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prelec, we appear to have the same text, the same document, the same content, if you will, in two different formats. One has a letterhead and a signature and a seal on it, which is Exhibit 56, and then the other has a different format, both purporting to come from Marko Rosic on the same date, in reference to again the same content of information. Can you provide any information to the Chamber about the -- these two different documents and how they might compare or what information you can provide, based again on your experience working with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, to begin with, they come from two different sources. The one labelled Exhibit 333.1 comes from the archive, as you pointed out, and this one, I believe, was submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor by the government of Bosnia, or at any rate some source other than the Croatian archive. The text is identical. The format is somewhat different. I can't speak to the most precise reasons why that will be the case, but I can say that, in my experience, I've seen many cases in which the same text has appeared in different formats, and many of those cases had in common with this one that one example would be, as the one currently on the ELMO, is signed and sealed, and has a hand-written number in a blank, and the other one is entirely machine-generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could we put the other one back on the ELMO, please. Now, let me also ask you, when you look at the B/C/S original, Exhibit 333.1, are you familiar with that format of document, and can you tell the Chamber what that appears to be?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This appears to be a document transmitted through an electronic system that is referred to as packet radio. I don't know exactly how this works. It appears to be something analogous to e-mail in which the characters are transmitted but not the actual image in the manner of a fax. So you couldn't transmit packet radio documents -- documents I've never seen transmit things like signatures or graphic depictions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. This might be considered something, as you said, either like a field e-mail or a field fax. Is that a fair characterization?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, on the original B/C/S document of 333.1, down in the lower left-hand corner of the page, if that can be moved up on the ELMO, please, do you see anything on that page -- a bit more, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can show the information, Mr. Usher, on the lower left corner somehow. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you see that, and does that indicate, in fact, some transmission information?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It indicates the abbreviation for main staff of the HVO in the top. This is a communications centre stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And a date and a time and a number of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It may be easier for the courtroom to look -- going back to the English version, where that same box of information is translated, this would indicate that a telegram was received, what's called here a telegram, on the 24th of April, 2300 hours, by radio connection. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, can you just confirm again for the Chamber, Mr. Prelec, you've seen other instances like this where you might have a situation where there is a field communication, then at some point, further documented by what we might call a signed, hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the Court's direction, let me flip through the documents. I'll try to be more selective in what I bring to the Court's particular attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me pause momentarily on Exhibit 457, if you can find that one. This is a -- appears to be a communication, at least over the typed name - I'm not suggesting for the moment whether that's Tuta's signature or not - but at least over his name, dated the 15th of June, 1993, to someone named Slobodan Bozic. Can you tell the Chamber, based on your research -- inquiries in this area, do you know who Slobodan Bozic is and the position he held on the 15th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the deputy director of the Department of Defence of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in terms of this request, again, over the author, commander of the special unit Convicts Battalion, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, indicating we hereby request the approval for promotion to a higher rank of the following Convicts Battalion members. Item number one is someone named Zeljko Bosnjak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I will leave to the Chamber's inspection the remainder of that list. Could I ask you to go to Exhibit 505. Can you just briefly indicate to the Chamber what that appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an order from Zlatan Mijo Jelic who signs as the commander of the 1st Light Assault Battalion of the military police, but was also at this time the commander of what was called the defence of Mostar sector of the South-East Herzegovina operative zone concerning the anti-terrorist group Mrmak ordering -- well, the text seems to imply it orders them to take 30 detainees from the Heliodrom Central Military Prison, although the content would seem to suggest that it's an order also to be taken by the custodian of those persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Indicating that 30 -- on the 8th of July, 1993, 30 prisoners from the Heliodrom should be taken for the Mrmak ATG. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just make one observation about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen a large number of these. What's curious about this one -- or suggest that perhaps it appears to be a sort of form letter allowing one to type in as needed day by day the information requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. It appears to be that the HVO did, in fact -- if you look at these and many documents like this which the Chamber can see, many examples included in this bundle, there seem to, in fact, be an HVO form for taking prisoners from the Heliodrom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. That's the point I was trying to make. When I said curious, I don't mean unusual. I mean simply worthy of note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can turn your attention to, in that regard, one other example of that, in particular -- maybe there may be two more examples. If you go to 591.1, and on this one --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the English translation of that document didn't get placed in the bundle. My apology. It was something that was a translation that did not come in until after the bundles were prepared. So if I can have the usher's assistance, please. This is the English translation of that 591.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll get the English translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're going to get it right now, Your Honour. There may be a few others as well. But I hope one of them is coming to you now. I just gave them to the usher. I gave them all to the usher. I'm sorry. I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to 591.1, does that appear to be, again, a similar document as the one we were just looking at, in fact, either the exact same form or very similar form for a different day, 5th of September, 1993, to take prisoners -- that prisoners be taken from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry, we found that there were -- all right. In a similar fashion, if I could ask the usher's assistance, please, to hand out 597.1, and we have those here, again, English translations of 597.1, Mr. President. Just to look at one more of these, I think for obvious -- what will be obvious reasons, although I will represent again to the Chamber that these -- it is not unique in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have 597.1, Mr. Prelec, can you see that this is -- can you confirm whether that again appears to be the same form, this one for the 12th of September, 1993, indicating that 30 prisoners be taken from the Heliodrom and placed in the personal responsibility of Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are some insignificant changes in format, but yes, it's basically the same form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the way, all these forms -- do you see the sentence, "The detainees are to be treated in accordance with the international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe this witness came to this Trial Chamber to tell us how he received certain documents from the Zagreb archives, the Croatian archives, the manner of his receiving those documents, and the documents speak for themselves. I strongly object to the Prosecutor going to just specific documents and asking this witness to read what the documents say. I thought he was here to tell us how he received these documents, the manner in which he received these documents and so forth. For that reason, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this witness has come here to assist us on which document we should look for and which part is more important, but I think that question, Mr. Scott, you asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- is not that proper, because the document could speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I agree with you, and I'm going to abbreviate this process now. I can assure the Court I'm not doing it for my benefit. I've read all these documents myself, but at some point it will be up to the Chamber to read all the documents and I'm just trying to give you some assistance. I think one thing this witness was able to confirm, in a shorthand way, is to confirm to the Chamber that the three examples of these forms of taking prisoners from the Heliodrom are just that, they are examples of many other similar documents the Chamber will Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. see when it has time to inspect the documents. With that, Your Honour, I will conclude the review of the documents in that binder. And of course, Mr. Prelec will be available for the Chamber's questions at the conclusion of counsel's questions on any of the documents, I suppose, if he can assist further. Mr. President, let me then turn to a second packet of documents. Actually, these documents also come from the Zagreb archives, but they are in a different set of documents, what we have called, and what you've heard us call the last couple of days, perhaps, is the international armed conflict binders. Could one of the packets of those documents be provided to Mr. Prelec, please? There should be -- it was a small packet. Yes, I think that's it. Mr. President, I'm now referring to the packet of about five documents that was distributed yesterday -- also one of the ones distributed yesterday. The first one on the top of the packet should be IAC-19.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Prelec, in addition to the documents we've been talking about so far this morning and yesterday afternoon, there is a -- five -- about five documents have been put in front of you, IAC-19, IAC-38, IAC-64, IAC-65 and IAC-67. And were you able to again confirm that -- through your inspections or review, that all those documents came from the Croatian state archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They all do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, on these, I just would simply direct the Chamber's attention again, simply by examples of the type of documents the Chamber will find in two binders of international armed conflict documents. If the Chamber could turn to IAC-38, you will find an order from the chief of the HVO General Staff Milivoj Petkovic dated the 12th of April 1993, in which he orders, "In order to have complete evidence and regulate the status of HV officers in the HVO, I hereby order, provide a list of all HV officers who are in your commands and units." I would also, as a further example, direct the Chamber's attention to IAC-64, dated the 8th of October, 1993, a report to the HVO main staff from Milenko Lasic. Directing the Court's attention to number 2, I will only read two or three sentences: "A mop-up of the terrain on Golubic was carried out today in a planned operation in Sector North."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If it please the Court, Your Honour, I object to the form of the question because I don't believe it is a question. Now, the Prosecutor, my learned colleague, is just taking documents and reading them, and the witness is sitting on the witness stand looking at the same documents. I object to this procedure, and I object to the form of the question because it is not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in the Chamber's hands. This is the way this has been done in a number of other proceedings at this Tribunal. Doesn't matter to me, frankly, one way or the other. It's only done to assist the Chamber. I'm happy to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, it should be in the form of question put to this witness. Otherwise, we don't need this witness at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. Again, I thought you had said a moment ago that I would -- that I, counsel, should point out the specific, the particular relevant parts, but all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, let's do it that way. Will you read the first three sentences of paragraph number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you could ask this witness what the first part of the paragraph 2 is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is it about, Mr. Prelec, the first three sentences of paragraph number 2?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns a -- what in the B/C/S would be an operacija ciscenja, which is a term that can be translated either as cleansing or as mopping up of terrain, in a particular area that's not familiar to me, in sector north, which is familiar to me, by the Tuta anti-terrorist group, and then it simply reports on, you know, things like losses and positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does it indicate to you that, in fact, after what would appear to be the initial action was over, that certain troops, certain units, took on the -- essentially holding responsibility, including components of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I apologise for being on my feet so much, but once again, I would ask for a continuing objection. The document will speak for itself. What it might indicate to this witness, since he's not an expert in the content of the documents but only where the documents came from, where he gained those documents, and the access to those documents, I think it's improper to ask the witness his opinion about what might be contained. The documents do speak for themselves, and it will be the ultimate issue for this Trial Chamber to decide, not this witness. And I object on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. We'll move on. I can understand that counsel would not -- hello?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We agree with you, Mr. Meek, on the most part of the objection. But on this occasion, we believe that it's about historical background, not the specific instance which is directly related to your client. So we have to give some leeway to the Prosecutor for him to ask questions that will guide us to the particular paragraph which they believe is important. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to dispense with the remainder of that binder as well, given the objections by counsel. I can understand, Mr. President, why the counsel would not like these documents. But of course, it will be up to the Chamber ultimately to read the documents, for each of Your Honours' own review, to the extent that they are admitted, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Whether I like these documents or don't like these documents is irrelevant, and Mr. Scott, I believe, knows that. The proper procedure for asking the questions of this witness is what is important to me for the procedure. And I take offence to the fact that Mr. Scott would make that statement in open court, that my objections are based on the fact that I might not like a certain document. To me, that's irrelevant. What is important is a proper procedure and what this witness can properly speak to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But we are not debating on those issues. I hope you could take the intentions from Mr. Scott in a good way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm moving now to the bundle in a blue packet of documents like this that is entitled "UNPROFOR Documents." And on these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Scott, could I ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We note here that those documents in the IAC numbers are not -- could you, after consultations with the Madam Registrar, give each a proper ID number at least, so that it could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have numbered, in order to simply identify these documents as distinct from what we call -- what the Prosecution team has called the chronological set of documents, which is the 17 binders preceded by the letter P, there are two additional specific binders of documents which have been provided to Defence counsel some time ago. We hope to tender the entire two binders to the Chamber in the near future and to distinguish these documents because they all go to the issue -- at least in part, they may have some other relevance as well. But principally for the purpose of establishing the existence of an International Armed Conflict, and we've simply put that -- called those IAC, and then IAC-1, IAC-2, on through those two binders of documents. We would intend to tender them that way. The additional P number can be placed on them if and when they are admitted, as I think has been the practice with other -- there is a second P or a P letter that is put on the documents when they are admitted. But it was simply to distinguish them as a distinct set of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we are satisfied with your explanation, but be sure during the break to consult with Madam Registrar concerning all those numbers, because all those documents are piling up. We just are afraid of in the future there might be some confusion with the numbering system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Clark has also a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, where we have those documents which you have called the International Armed Conflict bundle, and before you move on, could you ask this expert witness, who is after all, an historian, to explain to us the parties who are described in Document IAC-65. The Trial Chamber may not have the same familiarity with the names, seeing that they are in the International Armed Conflict bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, if you still have that bundle -- it has been taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher can give his assistance, again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can find IAC-65, and if you turn to -- maybe we can start with the last page or page 5. Are you familiar with the name Milenko Lasic and what his position was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the South-East Herzegovina Operational Zone. It was later renamed into the South-East Herzegovina Core District. But to the best of my knowledge, didn't change in substance when the name changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For what military force or organisation was that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, also directing -- if you look back to the first page, and throughout this document actually, there are references to something called the Tigrovi, translated in English "Tigers." Is that a name you have heard before?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the name of one of the guards' brigades of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention to several lines below that, there is the name Gromovi. Also, can you answer that in a similar fashion? Are you familiar with that unit?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's also the name of one of the guards' brigades of the Croatian army, although I couldn't tell you which number. They all have a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So in turn, they might have, for instance, 112th Brigade, or some other unit number apart from the name itself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Clark, I don't know if you have other questions about -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps in a similar fashion -- I appreciate Judge Clark's assistance. A similar question might be asked about IAC-67, might present a name or two that may not be as familiar to the Chamber, based on the evidence to date. If you would look at the second page of Exhibit IAC-67, do you see the author of that document? Can you state the name for the record, and tell the Chamber who that person was, what you know about him.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's Slobodan Praljak. He, at this time, the time of the document, was the commander of the main staff of the HVO. He had been, up until I believe May of 1993, one of the assistant ministers of defence of the Republic of Croatia and held a sort of commission office. He was on the commission for relations with UNPROFOR of the Republic of Croatia up until, I believe, September of 1993. A short time after this document, in November -- I think early November, he returned to Croatia, to the Croatian army, although I don't know if he actually took up a professional position thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And there, again, as we see on the B/C/S version of that document in the upper right-hand corner, we see an archival stamp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, putting that packet to one side. And then, if we could go to the next bundle, which is titled on the cover page in part --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm saying this because I'm going to ask, Mr. President, to go to private session on these documents for reasons I'll explain. But it's the bundle -- it's another one of these blue bundles like this. And part of it says -- the first part of it says "UNPROFOR BiH Command." If I could ask to go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that bundle in front of you, Mr. Prelec, are you familiar with, for instance, looking at Exhibit IAC-27?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the witness please be provided the bundle? The first one would be IAC-27. It will on the front -- the first document. They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit IAC-27, in the course of your work, at least at the ICTY and perhaps in other contexts as well, have you seen documents like this which indicate to be -- or appear to represent official records of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And looking at Exhibit IAC-27, does that appear to be, to your knowledge, consistent with the usual format and style, if you will, of UN records that are maintained in New York, like this and I'm sure many, many others?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very common, general-distribution document. It's available publicly at the UN headquarters building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If the Chamber will bear with me for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next ask you to skip down - just to cover all these at one time - skip down to Exhibit P239 in that same bundle? There will be two or three exhibits in between, but if you can find P239, can you say, sir, to the best of your knowledge, is that again an official UN Security Council report?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It appears to be a copy of a Security Council report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your similar attention to 239.1, is that again a UN publication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, where do we find the numbers on these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I hope they are down in the -- they should be down in the lower right portion of the documents, down in the right corner. There is an old -- Judge Clark, there is an old number, which may be confusing, my apology, up in the upper right corner, from another case. They should bear - I hope they bear - down in the lower right portion of the page, an additional P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: My little book doesn't appear to have any way that I can find my --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then there has been some error, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, are yours numbered? Do you have a 239.1?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's try to figure out what --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, Judge Clark. Admittedly, it is difficult without dividers. It's a bit difficult. The -- of course, in the full binders, again, the 17 binders that have been provided to the chambers, the binders -- the exhibits have been tabbed, I hope successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, going back to the question, if you can just put -- scan your eyes on 239.1, again, is that an official -- appear to you to be an official UN record?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, sort of later published or rather published in a different format version. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I think in that regard, going to Exhibit 349 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be the last -- all I can -- the only assistance I can hopefully give the Chamber is that it will be the last four pages of the whole bundle. So if you can just go to the very end of that bundle, I think you will find 349, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And a similar question as to that, Mr. Prelec: Is that again an official UN record?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, there are a couple -- there are several exhibits in this same binder which are not exactly of that same category, so if we can touch on those, Mr. President, this is the last -- the last questions I have for this witness, just so the Chamber knows timing-wise where we are so -- but if you can now find -- and, again, my apologies to the courtroom for the -- perhaps some difficulty, but if you can find Exhibit IAC-28, which is, I think, the second overall document in the binder, which is titled -- which is titled, "Special Assessment, Effects of Internecine Fighting between HVO and Muslim Elements," dated the 20th of January, 1993, going to someone named Goulding, United Nations, New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to confirm the source of this document, IAC-28?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor by UN headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can I direct your attention, please, to the next document, IAC-29? And again, this is an -- it says "Special Assessment, Central BH," dated 25th of January, 1993, to Goulding in New York, and can you tell us again, please, have you been able to confirm the source -- the origin of this document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same source.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is the UN?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. The enclosed report, is it correct, is the report itself that's enclosed under the -- excuse me, towards the middle of the page, subject, is it titled, "Croat Intentions for Provinces 3, 8 and 10"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Simply point that out to the Chamber as some -- to give some context in relation of the document to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you next look at -- if you leaf down considerably through this stack of the bundle of documents until you get to 265.1? I have two questions for you on that, Mr. Prelec, and I don't know to what extent you can guide us through this. If you had occasion to look at the source of this particular document, 265.1, or you may be able to indicate to us, in fact, that same document is included in one of the earlier UN records. So whatever assistance you can provide us about 265.1 would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a letter -- rather, a statement on Bosnian residency letterhead, statement of Alija Izetbegovic. I have seen this statement in a UN report. And that's normal practice often of the United Nations to transmit upon request statements of member states in official publications of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I'll just represent for purposes of time -- if I'm wrong, I'm sure counsel will correct me -- the text of that same document is included in the Security Council record, which has been marked as 239.1. I think there's only, Mr. President -- I think only two more documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to I think the next document, which is 271, titled "Joint Statement." On this document, Mr. Prelec, if you can, can you shed any light -- can you give any sort of background to the Chamber on this document, where it fits into the, if you will, what was happening in Bosnia as of late March, early April 1993? Not in detail, but just generally.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It's a proposed joint statement proposed by Mate Boban for signature by himself and Alija Izetbegovic concerning the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, certain specific actions to be taken, most significantly with regard to control over armed forces in six of the provinces, of the envisioned provinces. As you can see, it's actually signed by Mr. Boban but not by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your study concerning the conflict in Bosnia in 1993, can you tell the Chamber, to your knowledge, did Mr. Izetbegovic ever, in fact, sign that joint statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I direct your attention, finally, to the next document, 272. Can you tell us what that is. And to the extent you generally know, can you tell us how the OTP came to have that document, 272?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is a letter addressed to the president of Trial Chamber I; however, a copy of it was also submitted to Mr. Harmon by the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And that is simply a written confirmation by President Izetbegovic that, in fact, he did not sign the 2nd April, 1993 statement proposed by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that concludes my questions ... Let me just look. I have no further questions, Your Honour. To the extent any of those documents have not already been tendered, we will tender them, if I can do that. I can wait until after the remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Scott. Could I ask you to do a favour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We found at least four bundles or clusters of the documents we dealt with this witness. So during the break, could you please furnish us with a list, just a list only with the numbers on it, and you may have some indications of which cluster or which bundle they are, but just a list of all those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that we could have a clear picture to find the particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I will do that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just trying to catch up with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prelec. You have just mentioned the Vance-Owen plan in your last statement.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you read the Vance-Owen plan, as an historian?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. It would have been quite some time ago. I haven't consulted it recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me and the Trial Chamber if Izetbegovic signed that document, the Vance-Owen plan?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, this is somewhat tangled. I believe -- and I'm working from memory here -- that he did sign with a certain -- under pressure, as it were, although there was something peculiar about this. There was perhaps a feature of the plan that he did not approve of or did not sign, perhaps the map. But again, this would -- I'm perhaps not the best person to ask about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And from your testimony, it appears that you graduated from Harvard University. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then you received a doctorate from Yale?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And your thesis was written on what again, what was the subject?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want the specific subject or just the general?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The subject.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the origin of Yugoslav nationalism, specifically Yugoslav as opposed to Serb/Croat, and so on, at the turn of the 19th and 20th century, so in the territories of the Hapsburg monarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When did you conclude that? When was that finalised?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So during your research for that, you did not -- or did you -- study the breakup of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed it. It was taking place while I was studying. I never made sort of a -- at that time, while I was in graduate school -- really sort of rigorous study. It would have been very difficult also. The main sources of information that were available to me at that time were effectively media sources. There was a lot that could be gleaned from that, but it was somewhat limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, what date did you commence your employment with the Office of the Prosecutor here at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning of May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would it be a fair statement that since your -- since the beginning of May 1999, that you have studied the breakup of the former Yugoslavia to some extent?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I would like to clarify a few things for my own mind. When was it that you first began to collect documents from the Croatian archives in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was June of 2000, about that time, early summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber and me, please, how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I follow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you just -- for example, did you just go to Zagreb and ring at the front door and introduce yourself and say, I would like to look at some documents? Is that how it occurred?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This followed on an earlier brief period when some of the same documents were made available to me and others by the HIS, the Croatian information service. There were problems of a technical nature, where to inspect them, how to preserve the -- I suppose the operational security of the HIS. And as a result of that, the documents were moved to the Croatian State Archive, and we were told immediately, even before they had actually physically been moved, that that would be the place that they would be made available to us. The Croatian government would approve -- did approve lists of researchers who would have access. We would submit a list, and I was on that. And only those people could -- were granted access to the reading room where the documents were accessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That would have been when you first started out in June of 2000. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The HIS period was earlier, a month or two before. But the documents -- I believe it was June that we actually began working in the archive building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me ask this question: Tell me a little bit about this one- or two-month period before June of 2000 when -- what you call the HIS period. What was that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we requested access to what we referred to as the HVO archive. And we obtained from the Croatian government access, and it worked like this: We were collected at our hotel in the morning by several vans with a chase car, two chase cars, and driven to what was initially an undisclosed location. It later turned out to be a -- what you might call a safe house in the suburb of Samobor. That's about half an hour from Zagreb proper. And from there, there would be crates of documents that were responsive to a category that we had asked for, namely, documents on Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there for a moment. This town about a half hour from Zagreb, Samobor, you are indicating that -- would the HIS bring these documents to you after you made a certain request, your offices made a request? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And this lasted for about a month or two months?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it occupied that amount of time, but there were only, I think, eight or nine actual working days that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: At the safe house itself.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On two occasions, we had to stop because we were told the house was needed for other reasons, for work by defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned that Defence counsel for accused individuals at the ICTY had access equally to these documents, or did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, do you -- can you tell this Trial Chamber if you know from your own personal experience whether Defence counsel for Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic have had equal access to the documents as you have and your office has?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that for a substantial period of time, several weeks at least, fairly recently, this year, that I worked in the archive, there were two gentlemen who were pointed out to me by a colleague as, moreover by name, as investigators for the persons you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did -- did you have the occasion to go introduce yourself and confirm that statement that was made to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did see -- it's a fairly small room. I did see the name in question on order forms that we submitted, but no, I didn't introduce myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What is -- for my benefit and the Trial Chamber's benefit, what is the HIS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Croatian Information Service, which, as I put it yesterday, was a civilian intelligence agency charged largely with coordinating and analysing intelligence that was gathered, to a small degree by themselves, but mostly by other intelligence agencies of the Republic of Croatia. They were part of what was called the Office of National Security which was in turn directly subordinate to the president of the republic, as opposed to other services that would be within the Ministry of Defence, for example, or the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is it -- am I correct that you just stated that the HIS was an intelligence service, but it was gaining information and documents from other or many other intelligence services in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you name for the record some of these other intelligence agencies that HIS would receive documents from?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't testify to that they necessarily got documents, with the exception of the HVO documents, which were, it was represented to us by the Croatian government, moved to the HIS building on two separate occasions in 1996 and 1999. On other occasions, they would get information, possibly including documents, from -- well, in Bosnia, there was, for a short time, also an HIS office, but what was more important there was something called the SIS, the Security and Information Service, which was a part of the Ministry of Defence of the HVO. There was also an identical institution in Croatia. And they would also - and in fact they did also - submit information to the HIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would I be correct if I said, then, that the HIS was an intelligence agency that gathered information singularly and also from other intelligence agencies? Or did they just gather their information from these other agencies?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They do have, I believe, a small, autonomous intelligence-gathering capability of their own, but at least the way it's put in public, mostly they are supposed to get information from other services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And would the other services be only in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, or would they be from outside the country also?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under Croatian law, at least up until recently, the HIS has been the only service authorised to liaise with foreign intelligence agencies, but I really don't know to what degree that happened in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's 11.00. Would it be appropriate to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are adjourned until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, I think we were speaking about the HIS service before the break. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is this similar to the CIA in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way. The differences, I think, are obviously going to be -- or obviously are considerable, given the relative sizes and resources of the two countries in question. But in a way, certainly in that the CIA is also both an intelligence service in its own right and also a sort of umbrella service, or at least the director of Central Intelligence serves as a sort of coordinator for other American agencies. In that respect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You must have been very busy when you started the archive review in June of 2000. How many hours a day did you spend approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hours of the archive were -- their opening hours were from 8.00 until 4.00. Normally, it would take a little bit of time in the morning to get going, and we would take an hour break. So that would be approximately six and-a-half to seven hours a day of actual work time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And how many working days can you estimate that you were in Zagreb from when you started in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, although it's a rough guess, perhaps 40 to 50, if not more, from that time until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm looking at my notes to try to find -- yesterday, you mentioned that the sheer volume of these documents would be -- if placed side by side, the binders would be something like one to one and-a-half kilometres. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is that, again, page by page or binder by binder?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Binder by binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you personally review each of these binders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, how many people you had from the Office of the OTP at The Hague with you looking at these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll certainly represent, as a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, there has been a substantial number of persons and substantial -- I was going to say man hours, but I should say person hours -- involved in examining these documents. Having said that, I don't know the particular relevance of these questions to this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber does not believe that this question is relevant to the issue. You may skip your question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You also mentioned, Mr. Prelec, that you had an Office of the Prosecutor located in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are actually, at this point, three. There is a regular liaison office which handles official contacts with the Croatian government. There is an outreach office, which is simply a public relations office. And what's operative here, there was an office that was set up to handle the document flow, to do basically the same things that the Office of the Prosecutor does here in The Hague, namely stamp, index, and scan documents. This is what they do in that office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you say they scan the documents, are they scanning those into a computer?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are I believe put on to CD-ROMs, burned on to CD-ROMs as images.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your testimony that the documents had come from several locations before they arrived at the -- to HIS; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are two issues here. The documents at HIS came originally from a great number of locations from their originators, so various units of the HVO. The material in the Croatian archive itself Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. came from three major sources: those being the HIS itself, and then two large collections that were held by the Ministry of Defence, one just in regular Ministry of Defence offices and another at the Croatian naval base in Split, at Lora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did all these documents arrive, to your knowledge, at approximately the same time period at Zagreb, at the archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived over a period of approximately six or seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could you please tell me roughly when those six or seven months were?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they began to arrive in May and June of 2000, and I believe the last shipments from -- which were from the base at Lora, were at the end or toward the end of 2000 or the very beginning of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And since you commenced your study of these documents earlier, would it be a fair statement then while you were there in Zagreb, documents would keep coming in?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would. We couldn't access them until they had been catalogued in some rudimentary way so we would know what was available. So they would arrive, they would be processed by the archival staff, and then we would get an updated catalogue and we could then request them and work on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, do you have a list of different categories of the documents, at least for your own purposes or your office purposes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is actually -- I think this is what you might be referring to, this catalogue which I brought with me as a visual aid. It's simply the catalogue as it was prepared by the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But, for example, you would have handwritten letters, faxes, radio transmissions, computer-generated letters, letters originating from typewriters, those types of things?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no -- I don't really have a breakdown of those types of categories, although all those categories that you mentioned do exist in the archive. It's not organised in that fashion. It's organised by -- mostly by originator and substantive category, and not, you know, whether it's handwritten or typewritten or the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you then give me the substantive categories?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would take some time, but I can begin at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Some examples, then.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, the first part is the office of the President of Herceg-Bosna, so that is Mr. Boban. Then there was a category, a collection of the Department, later Ministry, of Defence of Herceg-Bosna. Then there was a large collection of documents of the main staff of the HVO. There are the four operative zones, operational zones. And I should say within most of these -- within the larger collections, there's a further breakdown. So for example, within the Vitez operational zone, there's a zone command subset, and then there are subsets for the brigades, the independent units, I believe the logistical base, things like this. And then sometimes there's a set of unsorted material that's just marked as various -- just loose papers that have been put into boxes. There's also -- there are two sets of Security and Information Service papers, one belonging to the Security Information Service headquarters, and its branch offices, and another belonging to Security Information Service officers attached to various units. Military police collection. As I mentioned last time, there was a small Armija Bosnia-Herzegovina collection and army of the Republika Srpska collection. There's assorted civilian institution collection, and also, finally, another miscellaneous category. There are also videotapes, audiotapes, maps, computer diskettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Before you -- before these documents arrived in Zagreb at the archive, you have no personal information, do you, or personal knowledge of what condition they were stored in or who had access to these documents prior to your seeing them, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know what was represented to the Office of the Prosecutor by the Croatian government on those points. But I wasn't there personally during their prior storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And during the prior storage, then, we really don't know who all had access to taking those documents or putting other documents in with them for the, say, six years' intervening period, do we?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything I can add to my previous -- we have representations from the government which state that they are based on interviews with some of the people who would have had personal knowledge. But I have no direct personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I believe that you had indicated in a response to one of my questions, or perhaps Mr. Scott, that with the previous government, there had been some problems with viewing these documents, previous Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm familiar with that there was extensive litigation beginning, I believe, in 1997. It's quite complicated, but all, in one way or another, a matter of record. Requests were made by the Office of the Prosecutor. A subpoena was issued. This was subsequently, I guess in a way, overturned. A binding order was issued, followed by other binding orders. But prior to our work in the Samobor house, to the best of my knowledge, these collections were in no way accessible to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, the Samobor safe house, did you find any documents during that short period of time that related to this case?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very few, I think. I recall, when I was reviewing the large binder that Mr. Scott presented, that some of the documents in that binder came from -- a few -- came from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So the bulk or majority, except for these few documents at the safe house in Samobor, were discovered or located by you or your team at the archives in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: With the problems that the OTP had occasioned with the gaining access to these documents, and you being a historian, is it possible that the previous government, between 1993 and January, early January, 2000, that the intelligence services for Croatia had created some documents to place in these binders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how I can answer that except as a theoretical possibility. Not having been present from 1993 through early January 2000, I can't exclude anything that would have happened, but, again, it's an issue of which I have no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So it is possible?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it as theoretically possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While you were -- first, let me ask you: Are you still going to Zagreb to search the archive there for documents that would relate to this case?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other members from the OTP staff who are still searching the Zagreb archives for documents that would be relative to this case?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor does have an ongoing presence, searching the archives, although it's a general search, so it's not specific to this case. It's merely a search for any documents that would bear on issues of relevance to the International Tribunal. That would include this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And very briefly, in this one and a half kilometres' worth of binders, can you give me a rough example of the sheer number of documents that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it in the low millions, so one, two million. It's difficult to say, since you can estimate the number of pages but many documents are multi-page so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So when you say one to two million, you mean documents, not necessarily pages; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the number of binders and the linear length I would estimate on the order of magnitude of about five million pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were at the archive during your time there in Zagreb, did you come across or view any documents which had to do with President Tudzman?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very few. There may have been -- there probably were one or two letters signed by President Tudzman, and there certainly were one or two letters addressed to him, and a larger number of communications that were addressed to a longer list of people including President Tudzman, but not very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So would it be a fair statement, then, that you never observed or came across at the archive any transcripts from any meetings that President Tudzman had?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anything at the Croatian state archive itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And today, as you testify, do you still work on the documents here at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you describe briefly your duties with these documents now?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I use them as a source. I -- in other words, I don't -- my duty is not to work on the documents per se. It's to do research on other questions that I suppose I probably shouldn't get into since they concern ongoing investigations, but in the course of doing that, I draw on the documents that we have here so far. I could give you an example. To establish who was in command of a particular brigade, I would review all the documents of that particular brigade, who they were taking orders from, sending orders to, reporting to, when one commander replaced another and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We hope your questions will be closely related to this case rather than the overall work schedule of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was ready to ask a question when the witness wanted to give me an example so I allowed him to give me an example. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've spoken about internal and external controls. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Consistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And is that the same term as using corroboration, as you would use, is consistency?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's similar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you give me a percentage of the documents that you have reviewed from the archive in Zagreb which you cannot find internal consistency with that document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, testing for internal consistency is a type of test that often doesn't yield results. If it's, for example, a printed document with no indicated addressee or sender, there's very little about the text itself that would indicate one way or another, so you would have to go to other types of tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would I be correct in asking you, though, with the external consistency, that is easier to prove or show?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I believe that your testimony is that you have reviewed these documents from the archive for external consistency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What documents in particular are you asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Any documents that might be admitted against my client.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only examined the particular binder for whether or not they originated from the archive itself. But I didn't make any specific detailed inquiries into those documents themselves for this purpose. A few of them, I've seen in other contexts and have examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So maybe you can't answer this question, but if you can't, just tell me. Is there a percentage of the documents which you've reviewed that you can corroborate externally or that you have corroborated by external means?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I think a couple of questions you asked are of a kind of fishing nature. It is not allowed to do this kind of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will -- he answered my question. He couldn't answer it, so I'll move on, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's particularly with the form of the question, rather than any particular questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: On some of the documents, Mr. Prelec, I've noticed that there may be a typed or computer-generated document, but then there's handwriting on it. Have you come across that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And on the occasions where there's handwriting on the documents, the typed or printed documents with no signature, do you have any way or means to tell who did that and when it was done?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in some cases, it's pretty clear with, you know, delivery notes, for example. Or there were some cases where a superior's order would actually be edited in pen or pencil for, then, retransmission further down the chain of command. In other cases, it would be more difficult to establish when or by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If the usher could help me with showing the witness document Exhibit Number P494 from the big binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is it this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
