utterances.text: Yes. It's from the Selected Zagreb Archive documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While she is looking for that, you have nothing to do with the translations, do you, from the Croatian version to English. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Sometimes I request translations, because they have to be official. But no, nothing itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Turning your attention, then, Mr. Prelec, to Exhibit P494, you see that there's a draft translation in English. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This is only a two-page document. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a two-page translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, translation. And that, the English version, translation version, on the second page, shows signature by Mladen Naletilic, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Yours sincerely, Mladen Naletilic," et cetera, and below it, it says, "Signature."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: "Signature." Now, would you please turn to the Serbo-Croatian version, the original, or a copy of the original? I can see that you're looking at it, Mr. Prelec.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, yes. I am looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That document looks like it was signed by Ivan Andabak, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first thing I would note would be that there appear to be two signatures, one above the line and one below, but I'm not a signature analyst, and since the stamp is over it, certainly the one above the line looks like it could be Ivan Andabak. Below it, I see a large T. It could be Tuta. I would have to look at it with some sort of magnification or perhaps a better copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Does the Office of the Prosecutor, to your knowledge, have in hand -- have a handwriting expert in their staff?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never met such a person, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would ask, Mr. Prelec, if you could turn in the same binder to Exhibit P601? There is also -- it's a one-page request dated 16 September 1993. And on the English translation, it shows "Mladen Naletilic-Tuta," and then underneath that, "/signed/," on the English version, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you please turn the page to the copy of the putative original document? I see that you're looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, yes. I should confirm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you read the signature, the actual signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel seems to be indicating that there is some inconsistency between the translation and the B/C/S document, and I would suggest to the Chamber that on looking at both the last two documents, this one and the last document that we were looking at, there is no inconsistency at all. It's simply the translation indicates the information, the typed information, on the document, and, for instance on 601, it gives the name, "Mladen Naletilic, Tuta," which as indeed we can all see, is on the B/C/S version, and then under that it just says, "Signed." There is no effort on a translation to create a signature, just indicates that the document is signed. It doesn't say if it's signed by Andabak or Tuta, and I think it's misleading to suggest that there is some consistent -- inconsistency in the way the document has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Court, could this be placed on the ELMO briefly? And I'll answer Mr. Scott. I'm not trying to indicate an inconsistency whatsoever other than to point out the fact that on the English translation, if one does not look close, it would appear that it was actually signed by my client. That's all I'm pointing out. I don't believe that it's necessarily inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is no dispute about that. I think the documents will show, and the Prosecution will not contest, that many of the documents were signed by Mr. Andabak. And we've never purported or attempted to mislead or show otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, now that you see on the ELMO we have this Exhibit P601, the original or a copy of what was the original document that was discovered at the archive, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In the upper right-hand corner would be the stamp that you've been referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That stamp, it's my understanding, would have been placed on the document when it arrived at the archive in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is only added during copying. I don't know if it's actually added to the photocopy or it's a feature of the photocopier itself but, no, they don't mark them in that way, the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to view some of the original documents at the archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We work exclusively with originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And on the originals, the stamp is not there; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's exactly right. It's simply noting that the copy comes from the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up. I didn't understand that. In your search for documents at this archive, if you know, how many of these documents did you find, such as Exhibit P601, that had a typewritten name of Mladen Naletilic but which was signed by Ivan Andabak or somebody else, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't put a number on it, but I did see a number of such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask this question; I think I know the answer. You've never seen my client sign any document personally, have you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a question: If there's a document that appears to be sent to an individual such as Mladen Naletilic, from, say, Lasic, how would you know if, in fact, Mr. Naletilic ever received that document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there had been a collection, which is something I never actually found, of Mr. Naletilic's own files collected in one place, that would, to me, suggest strongly such a conclusion, then I could make that for other persons. It would, again, depend based on the actual document in question where it was located. You could draw some conclusions based on the presence or absence of a transmission stamp. So, for example, if it was listed as being received at a place where Mr. Naletilic was known to be at a certain time, that would be a piece of valuable information. But -- or I suppose you could establish it in other ways. But what you could conclude with a very high degree of confidence, if you find it in the files of the sender, was that this was something that was meant to be sent. But what happened at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the other end, I suppose, there would be no additional information in the archive on that particular question. I'm sorry, there is one thing that you could add to that, if there were subsequent communication citing something like this, or responding to it in some way, whether it would be documentary or of some other nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excellent. So while you still have Exhibit P601 in front of you there, I think, there's nothing in the document itself, Exhibit P601, is there, Mr. Prelec, that would lead you to believe or reach any conclusion that Mladen Naletilic even had seen this document, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is -- this is a different issue. This is a document that was sent or purports to be sent from Mr. Naletilic to, in this case, the military police in Ljubuski. Now, I haven't examined this particular document to the degree of being able to tell you where precisely it was located, although I could do that. So it's a different issue that you're asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, it's a different issue. Let me ask this question: You agree that the document speaks for itself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You agree that the document is signed by apparently Ivan Andabak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So there's nothing -- my question is, there's really nothing that could tell you that Mr. Naletilic had any knowledge of this document being generated. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only qualification I would introduce would be it's a little easier with documents that come from a certain person. There was a collection -- I'm almost certain it's in the Department of Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which defence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Department of Defence file that indicated -- perhaps, I should say this in B/C/S and rely on the interpreters. [Interpretation] Units under the main staff. [In English] Wait for the interpretation here. Yes, that's correct. Which did include, among others, some files of Mr. Naletilic. So that would be the kind of external corroboration that had come from the person in question. And there are also similar documents found in the expected units actually of the main staff, for example. But strictly speaking, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to turn your attention for the moment to the binder of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I don't know whether we need to go into a closed session or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the ELMO lowered, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Prelec, I am Defence counsel Zelimir Par, and I represent, together with my colleague, Vinko Martinovic. The position of our Defence regarding these documents is that we completely rely on the documents that you have gathered, that is the Office of the Prosecutor has gathered, for two reasons. First, that we were unable to get any documents at all because we did not enjoy the appropriate cooperation from the authorities who keep them. And the second reason is that a number of these documents, an important number, constitute documents which are important to our Defence. For those reasons, I would like to ask you a couple of questions regarding the authenticity of this documentation. Please, doctor, are you familiar with the contents of all of these 17 binders containing documents that we received from the OTP just before these proceedings? Are you familiar with the substance?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all 17 binders. I reviewed the selection from the one binder that we've been looking at, although I'm virtually certain that there would be other binders -- documents within those 17 binders that I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question now is: Is it fair to say that practically each of these documents passed through your hands, that you checked each of them? Is it possible that any of these binders contain documents which you did not handle at all, either directly or in comparison with other documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't testify really about the 17 binders, since I'm not really acquainted with them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: We'll come back to these issues as to how these binders are formed in the first place. Could you tell us now which percentage of the documents you could say you haven't reviewed at all?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not acquainted with the totality of the documents that the Prosecution is using to put its case. I am acquainted very well with documents that come from the Croatian state archive, and I can say I have reviewed all of those. Some of those I located myself and held the originals in my hand. But I just simply have no knowledge of what is in the totality of those 17 binders, not really being a part of the team that put them together. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question is not too difficult. I don't insist upon each and every document. I'm more interested in the authenticity and the creation of these documents. So let's make one thing clear. With the method that you use in your work, can you personally guarantee that all the documents represented in a case like this are authentic insofar as they have been subjected to a certain scientific method verifying their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar with any sort of scientific or technological inspections that are made. But I can say that as a person who has dealt with an enormous number of documents, both here and elsewhere, I am overwhelmingly confident that the overwhelming majority of them are what they purport to be. I don't know if that's perhaps an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When I said scientific method, I meant precisely what you have described, comparison of documents and so on. A certain number of these documents that we have received from the Prosecutor do not bear a signature or a stamp, and this creates certain problems for us when we present these documents to witnesses. For instance, when we show a witness a list of names of members of a certain unit, there is no stamp or signature on the document. We present this document to the witness for purposes of confrontation with his own statement, and then the witness says, This document could have been created by anyone. It bears no signature or stamp. I would like to ask you who knows how these documents were procured, how would you deal with such an objection, namely, that the document could have been created by anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be very peculiar to find documents in a person's files that were simply created by some mischievous person. One might find drafts. One might often find several copies of the same document where one would have a signature and a stamp, and the remainder would not. And the very fact that one finds in the files of - just to take an example - the main staff, orders sent from the main staff allow one to conclude -- and then the same order somewhere else -- they are created in multiple copies, partly for archiving purposes. In fact, there was legislation, both in Croatia and in the Bosnian/Croat institutions, that required the creation of such multiple copies. So that would be my general conclusion as to why an individual copy might not have a signature or stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you for this exhaustive explanation. So we could conclude, couldn't we, that even documents like that which bear no signature or stamp are as reliable or authentic as any other document which does have a signature or stamp, if it's in this list?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the signature and stamp are added measures or indications of authenticity. But yes, I don't take them as being of great weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I would like to come back to one point which we have touched upon a moment ago regarding the way these binders are put together, binders for a specific case, that is. Are you personally familiar with the indictment against Vinko Martinovic? Do you know the details of that indictment?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in very general terms, having to do mostly with Mostar area. But no, actually, not really in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If you could elaborate a little. For such a case like that resulting from this indictment, how do you put together the documentation? You have reviewed a certain number of documents, and now these documents have to be sorted by various indictments, various cases. Do you, as an expert, process them according to your assignment, such as, for instance, please prepare for me documentation regarding Heliodrom, please give me everything on the command responsibility of Vinko Martinovic, et cetera? Is it -- is that the way in which you prepare the documentation for a specific trial, specific case?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the qualification that I am not the person who makes the final selection for the case. What I do analytically is to, in a case like this, divide it into three categories, and those would be documents of the person in question, so what -- that would indicate what that person was ordering or reporting or saying; documents to that person; and then often a very significant category, documents about, so documents that are neither from nor to, but that mention in some way. And it could be a very mundane way, simply saying -- I've seen many -- your clients, many references to, you know, the lines of defence in Mostar are as follows, a long list of various units with locations indicated, and then that would be -- that particular name would be within that. Also, police files and various kinds of reports based on those to which I would say they vary in helpfulness, some being extremely helpful and some being somewhat less so, depending on their proximity, at least to me as an historian, their proximity to the event. So the closer to the event in question, the more seriously I would take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe we should try and look at this using an example. Today, we have looked at three specific documents, orders, namely, issued by commander of the defence sector of Mostar, signed by Mijic, one was signed by Primorac, then commander of the 1st Light Assault Military Police. And these orders say that based on these orders, certain prisoners from the Heliodrom prison are sent to the Vinko Skrobo unit. And now, about the selection of documents, as I asked, documents are sorted by theme, so to speak. What I would like to know is in the course of your work on this case, have you encountered any other documents that would link Vinko Martinovic with Heliodrom? Have you encountered any other type of document, apart from these orders issued by other people, to the effect that people would be sent to his unit? Have you encountered documents corroborating that Vinko Martinovic had certain authorities within Heliodrom or something like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to clarify. I think the witness has tried to do this, but perhaps it is not fully appreciated. This witness is not -- if we can say it as such, he is not a member of the Tuta/Stela prosecution team. He did not participate in the selection or the organisation of 17 binders. He has seen many documents in Zagreb, some of which upon further investigation were relevant to this case. He went to Zagreb to work on various cases on behalf of the OTP. But there may be a misunderstanding that it is this witness who has somehow assembled the body of evidence in this case and is able to express some sort of views about that, and that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let us hear the answer of the witness about all those question. But this question is kind of a compound question. There are several questions. Let me see how the witness answers this question.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've done a lot of research on Heliodrom itself but not really any specific research on Mr. Martinovic. So what I could say is that there was -- there were actually several logs in which the Heliodrom administration would record when sets of detainees were taken out, and they would record generally the dates, the authorising person, the person who collected them, and whether or not something had happened, whether they had been shot and killed or shot and wounded or in some cases not returned after -- when they were supposed to be returned. I do recall seeing the Mrmak or Vinko Skrobo unit cited, and I actually made a count of how many times this happened, but I don't remember now off the top of my head how many times that was. I may have left part of your question out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: All right. I'll try to clarify this briefly. You say that you have studied Heliodrom. You must have paid the most attention to who was responsible, which persons or units were responsible, or in charge of the operation of that system or camp or whatever you want to call it. Have you ever encountered any documents which would indicate that Vinko Martinovic would be the person who had any powers whatsoever within that camp?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any documents indicating that he had a sort of formal command authority or something of that nature. But one of the things that I saw repeatedly in regard to Heliodrom was a sort of complaint by the warden or his deputy, and those would be -- well, it's not important -- that various types of people were coming in and behaving in various improper fashions, be it in some cases stealing from the detainees or taking them out or in some cases removing and liberating -- this was in most cases Croat detainees, of whom they were a few. And I think there was -- there may have been some mention of your client. So I can't right now testify that that was certainly the case, but since you asked me whether that was not the case, I can't confirm that either. I think it was that he was mentioned in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question referred to real authority, and what you mentioned goes outside that scope, but I'll accept that there are such other documents. It is very important to me, as a member of the Defence team, to know what exactly are those documents that are not available to us, because I am in a position where I know about documents that exist and I'm not aware of the existence of other documents that you may have at your disposal and which may shed a different light on what we are discussing here today. And that is the thrust of my questions. In that context, I would like to put to you another question. Just as we spoke of Heliodrom, certain documentation must also have been gathered regarding the Bulevar, the line of demarcation. Have you perhaps studied that subject as well? And are you in a position to answer this question? Have you ever seen a document which would indicate that the Vinko Skrobo unit was stationed or active on any position other than the Health Centre on the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see documents that listed what units were in what places along the line of confrontation in Mostar. I can't recall what the precise location of the Vinko Skrobo unit was now, although those documents could be - I assume probably already are - available. The -- I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't think it was expressed as a single building. I think it was - in fact I'm certain, almost certain - that it was from this location to another location. So, for example, from the Bulevar to some other intersection or building. But I wasn't really -- I never focused on that in my own analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Please, when I said the Health Centre, I didn't only mean that particular building alone but the surrounding area as well. My purpose was to determine whether the documentation available to the Office of the Prosecutor clearly indicates that zone. Is it clear in the documentation of the Prosecutor? I understand that you personally may not have dealt with these issues, but you could direct us to the person who did. Is it possible to derive this from the available documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... these documents, as I think has been noted, continue to arrive, and I really don't recall the -- at what particular point the ones that I was referring to have arrived here. Also, they are of some real value but it's of limited value because they note what the units in question are responsible for, which obviously doesn't mean that they are necessarily there 24 hours of every day. It's their job, so to speak, that's described. So I don't think you could necessarily rule out the possibility that individual members or indeed organised groups of a certain unit appeared elsewhere. But as far as what the Office of the Prosecutor had bearing on that question, and when they had it, I couldn't -- certainly couldn't even begin to answer now, but it could be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So we will agree on this. I accept it when you say that there is a possibility that members of some unit abandoned that particular position and go somewhere else. But let us also agree that the unit as such cannot abandon that position because, if it does, the enemy will break through and the town will fall. I therefore believe it is very important to determine whether a certain unit was supposed to hold a certain location. If it abandoned that location, either it had to be replaced by some other unit or that location will fall. But let us not dwell on that. I repeat my question: The documents that we received from the Prosecution with regard to the line of demarcation are consistent enough, and are there other documents, because it is you who told us today that the entirety of this documentation should be checked for consistency. Are there any other documents which would not be consistent with what we have been given?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, there is a misunderstanding apparently of the scope of this witness's work. He did not select these documents, he did not make a compilation or come prepared to testify about opinions and what the documents show. On direct examination, I did not ask this witness to express a single opinion as to had he reviewed a collection of documents and come to a conclusion. I could have asked him, I suppose, "Have you ever reviewed documents and do you think Vinko Martinovic is guilty?" Well, he could give his opinion. I obviously haven't done that. But that's not the nature of the work that he's been asked to do. He went to Zagreb, he and others brought back documents back from Zagreb. He looked at a list that's been marked as Exhibit 883 and was able to verify that those documents came from Zagreb. Now, I can tell the Chamber that the persons who selected the exhibits that make up the 17 binders were myself, Mr. Bos, Mr. Stringer, and Mr. Poriouvaev. Certainly, we have an opinion as to what they show. I assume you don't want us to say that opinion at this time. But it's not appropriate to ask this witness to express an opinion on work that he's never performed. There is a misunderstanding -- I'm sorry, there is just a misunderstanding of what this witness can do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par? Did you hear the explanations by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honour, I would like to respond briefly. I believe that this indictment is based on two things. One is testimony in the courtroom and the other is documents. Also, on the same basis, I believe that we have here in the Court with us today a person who is competent enough to share with us all the basic information about these documents, their authenticity, their usefulness, and what I'm particularly interested in here, their consistency. I would particularly like this person to tell us what has been made available to us and what has not. I don't want this witness to give us conclusions about someone's responsibility. I'm only asking him about the consistency and authenticity of certain documents. The purpose of all my questions was to establish whether they had been subjected to that scientific method and whether there are any other documents that we don't know of. I would like the Trial Chamber to allow me to put another question regarding these documents; namely, the person mentioned in the documents used today in the cross-examination [as interpreted] by Mr. Prosecutor. Was the position of command responsibility on the line of demarcation studied, one; two, the person, Zlatan Mijo Jelic signed as the commander of defence, sector Mostar, was his command responsibility a subject of interest in the review of documents; and what are the powers inherent in this position of defence sector commander? Those are the questions that I would like to put to this witness, with the indulgence of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fairly complicated question which I have not really rigorously examined. One of the things that I was actually planning on doing in -- for other reasons. But it is familiar to me, and this is based on a document that I have reviewed, since it was one of the ones that was put to me, that in the very early July, the Mostar area was further subdivided into three sectors, the central one of which was the so-called defence of Mostar sector. Now, in the implementing order, which was signed by both Mr. Stojic, the director of defence, and General Petkovic, the chief of the main staff, the commanders of those three sectors were given extensive authority over civilian and military units in their areas and, moreover, subordinated in some fashion to the main staff. But this is simply what is reflected in the document in question. I don't recall the exhibit number, but it's a document of the 2nd of July. Now, how exactly that worked, since this was laid over an existing command structure involving various units, how that worked in practice is something that is not known to me. But it does seem clear that the individual who you mentioned, Mr. Jelic, did have serious authority in this territory. I'm not sure how much further I could really go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Prelec. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, in terms of the overall access that was gained to this HVO archive, there has been quite a bit of testimony on that. Is it the case that during the time that the Republic of Croatia continued to be governed by what might be called the Tudjman regime -- is it correct that during the time that the Republic of Croatia was governed by the Tudjman regime, that no access to this material was given to the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I think we received several discrete documents that were of very, very little significance. But as far as access to the collection itself, no, there was nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was after the change of governments when Stipe Mesic was elected the president of Croatia that the policy toward the Tribunal changed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it began in a way with the appointment of a new government, which was a little bit before the election of Mr. Mesic. But yes, basically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct to say, and can you assist the Chamber in confirming that in your dealings and the dealings of the Office of the Prosecutor with senior Croatian officials, that they confirmed and characterised this collection of documents as the HVO archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. There was never any suggestion that it could be anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me give you several certain individual names. Are you familiar with the name Dr. Ozren Zunec?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the first half of 19 -- excuse me, 2000, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was initially a professor at the University of Zagreb, and then was appointed the director of the HIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So he at that time, at the time that the Office of the Prosecutor gained access to these documents, Dr. Zunec was the chief of this Croatian information service that you've told us about today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he one of the persons who confirmed to you and to other representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor that this was the HVO archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall him saying it in exactly those words. But I had very extensive discussions with him about the HVO archive, and it was simply absolutely clear that this is what it was, in his view, and those of the other relevant persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was another senior Croatian official involved in the Office of the Prosecutor gaining access to these documents, the deputy prime minister of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Goran Granic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did Dr. Granic, the deputy prime minister of Croatia, ever indicate any doubt to you that these were, in fact, the documents from the HVO, or to other representatives from the Office of the Prosecutor, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber who Mr. Orsat Miljanic is?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orsat Miljanic is the chief of the Office of Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal and the International Court of Justice of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is his full-time professional and official job on behalf of the government and Republic of Croatia to act as the chief liaison officer with this Tribunal and with the International Court of Justice? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And has Mr. Miljanic been involved in the transmittal and making available of these documents that are included in the collection you've reviewed as senior official representative of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, he was directly involved in that I would collect copies from his office. He was there personally. And now it's under the auspices of his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Chamber may be curious to know, prior to Dr. Ozren Zunec being placed the head of HIS, who was his immediate predecessor? Maybe not immediate, but in the latter part of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe his immediate predecessor was Miroslav Tudjman, who was, of course, the son of the late president. And prior to him, Miroslav Separovic, although a small possibility I've gotten the order wrong. I'm pretty sure it was Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it correct to say that Mr. Miroslav Tudjman, not to be confused with his father Franjo Tudjman, was the head of this agency which had the HVO archive in its possession which had, prior to that time, not been produced to the ICTY, despite numerous requests and binding orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must object to the form of that question. I don't think it's proper for this witness. He didn't come to work for the OTP until 1999, and this well precedes this witness's work with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear the answer from this witness, even if it's hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a substantial period of time while I was here that there was no access, and this was a time, indeed, when Miroslav Tudjman was the head of the agency. But it's a matter of record that I've had access to that this had been the case prior to my arrival here. So the answer to your question would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time. I had hoped we'd finish with this witness today, but I assume the Chamber might also have some questions and I have a few more questions. So I suppose we might as well continue on Tuesday morning. But I'm in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm very sorry that we could not finish this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness today. Actually, it's just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in the Chamber's hands. I'm happy to proceed for -- I think I can finish my questions in five -- in not more than five minutes, but I know sometimes the Chamber does not want to go past the appointed time. But I'm completely in the Chamber's hands, if you would like to finish, go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultations with the Judges and with the Court deputy, Madam Registrar, we will adjourn today until 9.30 Tuesday morning.
